title: Module 3: Legal Responsibilities – Privacy, Documentation & Consent

questions.stem: Which legislation governs personal health information in Ontario?
options: The Motor Vehicle Act
The Occupational Health and Safety Act only
The Canada Labour Code
PHIPA
questions.explanation: The Personal Health Information Protection Act, 2004 governs personal health information in Ontario.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which legislation addresses consent to treatment in Ontario?
options: The Residential Tenancies Act
The Municipal Act
The Environmental Protection Act
The Health Care Consent Act
questions.explanation: Consent to treatment is governed by the Health Care Consent Act.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which framework is the correct starting point when the question is "Who may access or receive this report?"
options: The employer's social committee
Personal preference
PHIPA and authorized processes
The patient's family's wishes alone
questions.explanation: Access and disclosure decisions are governed by PHIPA and the custodian's authorized processes.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which framework is the correct starting point when a patient asks to stop scanning?
options: HCCA and consent standards
The scheduling policy alone
The equipment manual
The billing code
questions.explanation: The patient's request to stop is a consent matter governed by the HCCA and consent standards.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which legislation is the correct starting point when a child may need protection?
options: PHIPA alone
The MRIT Act alone
Workplace scheduling policy
The Child, Youth and Family Services Act
questions.explanation: Child protection reporting duties arise under the CYFSA.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: A concern about sexual abuse by a regulated professional triggers reporting duties under which legislation?
options: PHIPA alone
The HCCA alone
Local hospital policy only
The Regulated Health Professions Act
questions.explanation: Reporting duties for sexual abuse by a regulated professional arise under the RHPA.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: How do the RHPA and the MRIT Act relate to a practice question?
options: They govern only hospital construction
They apply only outside Ontario
They provide Ontario's professional regulatory framework for this profession
They are unrelated to professional practice
questions.explanation: Together they form the regulatory framework establishing scope, titles, authorized acts, and reporting duties.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: How do CMRITO standards relate to a documentation question?
options: They have no connection to documentation
They apply only to physicians
They provide the professional expectations for how records are kept
They replace PHIPA entirely
questions.explanation: The regulator's documentation standards set the professional expectations for records.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: A learner must connect a practice question to the relevant law or standard. Which approach is best?
options: Identify the subject of the question — information, consent, documentation, protection, or regulation — and match it to the corresponding framework
Choose the shortest title
Assume all laws are the same
Ignore the law and follow habit
questions.explanation: Matching the subject matter of the concern to the correct framework is the taught approach.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes PHIPA from the HCCA?
options: PHIPA concerns treatment; the HCCA concerns information
PHIPA concerns information; the HCCA concerns consent to treatment
They are identical statutes
Neither applies to sonographers
questions.explanation: PHIPA governs personal health information while the HCCA governs consent to treatment.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which pairing is CORRECT?
options: "Who may receive the report?" → workplace seniority rules
"The patient asks to stop" → equipment policy
"How do I record what happened?" → CMRITO documentation standards
"A child may need protection" → PHIPA only
questions.explanation: Documentation questions are answered through the regulator's standards.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: What is the role of a standard in answering a legal-responsibility question?
options: It replaces all legislation
It translates legal requirements into professional expectations for practice
It applies only after a complaint
It has no legal relevance
questions.explanation: Standards operationalize legal duties in everyday professional work.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: A student is unsure which framework applies to a request for patient information from an insurer. What is the best response?
options: Share the information because the request is official
Share whatever the insurer asks for
Apply PHIPA and the formal release process for third-party requests
Ignore the request entirely
questions.explanation: Third-party requests such as insurers follow PHIPA and the formal release process.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: Which statement about the interplay of laws and standards is TRUE?
options: All frameworks can be used interchangeably
Each framework has a distinct starting point, and identifying the right one guides a defensible response
Only PHIPA ever applies in an echo lab
Standards have no role once legislation applies
questions.explanation: Selecting the correct starting framework leads to an appropriate, defensible response.
tags: Which Rule Applies? Legal and Professional Frameworks

questions.stem: What is personal health information (PHI)?
options: Information that identifies someone and relates to their health or care
Any information found in a hospital
Information about a hospital's budget
Information that identifies someone but has no health connection
questions.explanation: PHI is identifying information connected to an individual's health or care.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: What is a health information custodian (HIC)?
options: Any employee with a login
Any patient's family member
Any member of the public
A hospital or certain healthcare providers with custodial responsibility for health information
questions.explanation: HICs — such as hospitals and certain providers — are legally responsible for personal health information.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: How should staff and students handle personal health information?
options: According to personal judgement alone
Through personal accounts and private groups
Within the custodian's authorized processes
Only if the patient is famous
questions.explanation: Staff and students act within the custodian's authorized processes for handling information.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Which statement best defines privacy in this context?
options: The patient's rights and interests in how their information is handled
The professional's duty to protect information
The employer's data storage policy
The ability to keep secrets from the care team
questions.explanation: Privacy refers to the patient's rights and interests regarding their information.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Which statement best defines confidentiality?
options: The professional duty to protect information and share it only with authority
The patient's right to demand silence
The employer's right to publish records
A courtesy that may be ignored when busy
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is the practitioner's duty to safeguard information and disclose only with authority.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: How do privacy and confidentiality relate?
options: They are identical terms
Privacy applies only to paper records
Privacy is the patient's right in how information is handled; confidentiality is our duty to protect it and share only with authority
Confidentiality applies only to physicians
questions.explanation: The two concepts are complementary — one is the patient's right, the other the practitioner's duty.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Which action best protects a patient's privacy during a busy day?
options: Discussing cases at the nurses' station with doors open
Moving care conversations away from public areas
Leaving workstations unlocked for convenience
Sending information through personal messaging apps
questions.explanation: Care conversations should occur away from public areas to protect privacy.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Which statement about information in an echo appointment is correct?
options: Only disclosure needs authority
Collection never requires authority
Every step — collection, use, and disclosure — needs an appropriate purpose and legal authority
Use of information is unrestricted once collected
questions.explanation: PHIPA applies to each step of handling information, not just disclosure.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Obtaining a relevant history from a patient is an example of which PHIPA step?
options: Collection
Disclosure
Destruction
Sale
questions.explanation: Gathering relevant health information from the patient is collection.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Reviewing the referral to prepare for the scan is an example of which PHIPA step?
options: Use
Disclosure
Collection from the patient
Destruction
questions.explanation: Using already-held information for the purpose of preparing care is "use."
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Sending patient information to another authorized recipient is an example of which PHIPA step?
options: Collection
Disclosure
Use within the care team only
De-identification
questions.explanation: Providing information to another authorized recipient is disclosure.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: Which statement about a student's access to a record system is correct?
options: A login means any record may be opened
Students may open any record for learning
Authorization is irrelevant for students
Technical access operates within the custodian's authorized processes and does not itself authorize any particular access
questions.explanation: Access must be within authorized processes and supported by an authorized purpose.
tags: Personal Health Information, Custodians, Privacy and Confidentiality

questions.stem: What is the circle of care?
options: The healthcare setting's physical layout
The network of roles that may be involved in providing or helping provide the patient's healthcare
The patient's family and friends
Any group with a hospital login
questions.explanation: The circle of care describes roles involved in providing or helping provide healthcare to the patient.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Under what condition may a custodian rely on assumed implied consent?
options: Never under any circumstances
Only when the patient is unconscious
When PHIPA's conditions are met
Only for family members
questions.explanation: Assumed implied consent may be relied on when the statutory conditions of PHIPA are satisfied.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: What must be true of the purpose for relying on implied consent?
options: The purpose must be providing or helping provide healthcare
The purpose must be curiosity
The purpose may be personal interest
The purpose may be entertainment
questions.explanation: Only a healthcare-provision purpose supports reliance on implied consent in the circle of care.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Which roles can be relevant members of a patient's circle of care?
options: Clinicians and assigned support staff involved in the patient's care
Any employee in the building
Social media followers
Strangers who ask politely
questions.explanation: Relevant roles include clinicians and assigned support staff participating in the patient's care.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: What must be done when the patient has communicated a known consent restriction?
options: It may be ignored for efficiency
It applies only to family
The known restriction must be addressed before relying on implied consent
It is irrelevant to disclosure
questions.explanation: Known consent restrictions must be respected and addressed before information is shared.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: For a cardiac echo appointment, who would generally be involved in the patient's circle of care?
options: A nurse who is not involved in the patient's care
An insurer requesting results without authorization
A family member waiting with the patient, absent permission
The cardiologist who ordered and will review the echo
questions.explanation: The ordering and reviewing cardiologist is clearly within the patient's circle of care.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: A sonographer declines to discuss a patient's results with a coworker who is not involved in the patient's care. Which concept does this best illustrate?
options: Privacy
Implied consent
Circle of care
Confidentiality
questions.explanation: Declining to share with someone outside the care relationship exemplifies the duty of confidentiality.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Does implied consent permit sharing information with anyone who asks?
options: No — the purpose, role, and conditions must support the disclosure
Yes, if the person asks politely
Yes, for all family members
Yes, whenever the unit is busy
questions.explanation: Implied consent is conditional — it requires an appropriate healthcare purpose and an eligible role.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: A friend of the patient asks for the echo findings at the reception desk. What should staff do?
options: Share the results because the friend drove the patient
Share verbal summaries only
Share the full report without checking
Confirm permission or other lawful authority before any disclosure
questions.explanation: Friends are not automatically within the circle of care; permission or lawful authority must be confirmed.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Which statement about students and the circle of care is correct?
options: Students may access anything for educational purposes
Students are exempt from privacy rules
Students work within the custodian's authorized processes and their assigned care role
Students may share cases informally with classmates
questions.explanation: Student access is governed by the same authorized processes and care-purpose requirements.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: A receptionist assigned to the patient's care pathway accesses information needed to arrange follow-up. What matters most in assessing that access?
options: Whether the receptionist has a clinical degree
Whether every employee can open the record
The role, purpose and authorization for the access
Whether the patient is well known in the community
questions.explanation: The decisive factors are role, purpose, and authorization — not job title alone.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: What is the correct interpretation of implied consent in an echo setting?
options: It may sometimes be inferred from conduct in context, but all requirements for valid consent still apply
Arrival alone equals full consent to everything
Silence always equals consent
Lack of resistance equals consent to share information with anyone
questions.explanation: Implied consent is contextual and still subject to the requirements of valid consent.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about arrival for an appointment?
options: Arrival automatically authorizes every disclosure
Arrival waives the right to ask questions
Arrival ends the need for explanation
Arrival, silence or lack of resistance alone is insufficient to establish consent
questions.explanation: Passive presence alone does not constitute informed consent.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Before an echo, what does the taught approach require regarding implied consent?
options: Begin scanning immediately
Explain the examination and ask permission to proceed
Assume consent from the order alone
Skip explanation if the patient is a repeat client
questions.explanation: Even where implied consent may apply, the examination should be explained and permission sought.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: A colleague says, "The patient is in the circle of care, so I can share anything." What is the best correction?
options: The colleague is entirely correct
Nothing may ever be shared
All information may be shared with any clinician
Only the information authorized for that purpose and role may be shared — share only what is needed
questions.explanation: Circle-of-care sharing is limited to what is authorized and necessary for the purpose.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates appropriate reliance on implied consent?
options: An unrelated colleague opens the chart out of curiosity
A student opens records for entertainment
The reporting cardiologist opens the echo images to interpret the study
A visitor browses records while waiting
questions.explanation: Interpretation of the study is a healthcare purpose by a relevant role — the classic authorized access.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: What is the key flaw in reasoning that "the login permits the access"?
options: Logins are always unreliable
Logins should never be used
A login does not answer "may I look?" — the authorized purpose must support the access
Logins authorize curiosity-based access
questions.explanation: Technical ability to access must be distinguished from authority to access.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: Which condition of relying on assumed implied consent is correctly stated?
options: Any purpose is acceptable if the person is employed in healthcare
The purpose must be providing or helping provide healthcare, the role must be relevant, and known consent restrictions must be addressed
Known consent restrictions may be ignored
Roles are irrelevant once a login exists
questions.explanation: The conditions concern purpose, role, and respect for known restrictions.
tags: Circle of Care and Implied Consent

questions.stem: A caller from a referring physician's office asks for a patient's echo report. What should be verified FIRST?
options: Whether the caller is pleasant
Whether the patient is popular
Whether the request arrives by email
The caller's identity, role, and the care purpose of the request
questions.explanation: Requests from referring offices require verification of identity, role, and care purpose before any disclosure.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: A patient's daughter asks for the results of the echo. What is the correct understanding of "lawful authority"?
options: Lawful authority means a legal basis for sharing — family relationship alone does not automatically give access
Being someone's daughter automatically provides lawful authority
Family members may see any record at any time
Only written consent from a lawyer is required
questions.explanation: A family relationship by itself does not establish permission; a legal basis must be identified.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: How should a sonographer determine whether information may be shared with a capable patient's daughter?
options: Share automatically because the daughter drove the patient
Share automatically because the daughter looks worried
Never share with family under any circumstances
Ask the patient directly, for example, "Are you comfortable with me discussing your examination with your daughter?"
questions.explanation: For a capable adult, permission should be sought from the patient directly.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: What is the best opening line when you are unsure whether a request for information may be fulfilled?
options: "Sure, I'll send everything we have."
"I'm not allowed to talk to anyone."
"Let me check my personal messages first."
"I need to verify your request and confirm what information I'm authorised to share."
questions.explanation: Verifying the request and the scope of authorized sharing is the professional response when permission is unclear.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: An insurance company requests a patient's echo findings. What is the correct process?
options: Email the report immediately
Provide verbal results to any representative
Use the formal release process, generally with the patient's express consent
Share because the insurer paid for the test
questions.explanation: Insurer requests follow the formal release process and generally require the patient's express consent.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: A patient cannot make the decision about sharing their information. What must be verified?
options: Who is legally authorized to act as the substitute decision-maker, and the authority and its limits
Who is the oldest family member
Who has the loudest voice
Who paid the bill
questions.explanation: The SDM's legal authority — and the limits of that authority — must be confirmed before disclosure.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: Which statement about sharing information in a care setting is correct?
options: Share the entire chart whenever a clinician asks
Share verbally without documenting
Share only the information authorized for that purpose, through the approved process, within your role
Share only if the patient is not present
questions.explanation: Disclosure must be limited to what is authorized and necessary for the stated purpose.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: A curious coworker asks to see a patient's images. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Show the images because you work in the same organization
Show the images if they promise not to tell
Show the images because they are a friend
"I can't share those images for that purpose. If you're interested in learning, we can look at an approved teaching example."
questions.explanation: Working in the same organization does not authorize access; approved teaching examples protect both patient and learner.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: What is the correct response if you are unsure whether opening a particular record is legitimate?
options: Open it quickly and close it afterward
Ask your supervisor or the designated privacy resource before accessing it
Open it because you have a login
Ask a classmate for an opinion and then open it
questions.explanation: Saying "I need to check before I do that" is the professional response when permission is unclear.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: A sonographer can technically open a patient's catheterization report but works only in the echo lab. What is the correct understanding?
options: Any chart in the system may be opened
Access is authorized if you are curious
Access is authorized if you are a student
Technical access does not authorize access outside your authorized activities
questions.explanation: Access must relate to authorized activities; opening unrelated records can breach confidentiality.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: What should a sonographer do if they want to review a catheterization report for learning purposes?
options: Open the report independently because it is educational
Ask a supervisor to arrange a supervised or authorized review
Print the report for personal study
Email a copy to classmates
questions.explanation: Educational review should be arranged through authorized, supervised processes.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: A relative is adamant that they be told the results, but the patient has asked for privacy. What governs the response?
options: The relative's seniority in the family
The patient's privacy and any permission they have given — the relative's insistence does not override it
Whoever argues loudest
The relative's transportation contribution
questions.explanation: Even when a family member is insistent, the patient's stated wishes and lawful authority govern disclosure.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: What is the "minimum necessary" principle in this context?
options: Share as much as possible in case it helps
Share nothing under any circumstances
Share the whole record for completeness
Share only what is needed for the authorized purpose
questions.explanation: An examination referral does not justify browsing or sharing unrelated parts of a person's information.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: Which statement about a substitute decision-maker and information is correct?
options: An SDM may receive every detail without verification
An SDM is the same as any family member
No verification is required if the SDM appears confident
Verify the SDM's authority and its limits before sharing; an SDM's authority is not unlimited
questions.explanation: The SDM's legal authority and its scope must be confirmed before disclosure.
tags: Access Decisions and Requests for Patient Information

questions.stem: While scanning, the door opens and the patient's chest is partially exposed. What is the best response?
options: Ignore the interruption and keep scanning
Shout at the visitor
Pause, cover the patient, ask the person to give you a moment, close the door, check comfort, and confirm readiness before continuing
Finish quickly without covering the patient
questions.explanation: Pausing to protect dignity with a calm, clear request preserves the patient's privacy and comfort.

questions.stem: A colleague asks about a patient's findings within earshot of other patients. What should you say?
options: Answer loudly so everyone hears
Refuse ever to discuss the case
"Let's discuss that somewhere private" — and still confirm they are authorized to receive the information
Write the findings on a whiteboard
questions.explanation: Move the conversation to a private location and separately confirm authorization to share.

questions.stem: What should a practitioner do whenever they step away from an active workstation?
options: Leave it open for convenience
Lock the session
Minimize the window only
Ask a colleague to watch without locking
questions.explanation: Locking the workstation prevents unauthorized viewing while you are away.

questions.stem: How should confidential paper material be disposed of?
options: In the regular recycling bin
In the general trash
Left on the desk
Through the approved secure disposal process, such as a designated shredder bin
questions.explanation: Confidential material must be disposed of through the designated secure process.

questions.stem: Which habit best protects privacy in a busy department?
options: Assuming walls are soundproof
Speaking about cases wherever there is space
Leaving records open for the next person
Noticing who can see, who can hear, and who has access
questions.explanation: Actively noticing visibility, audibility, and access builds reliable privacy habits.

questions.stem: A student posts an echo image with the name removed but the caption includes the patient's age, hospital unit, and unusual finding. Why is this still a problem?
options: Private groups are always part of the circle of care
The combination of details may identify the patient, and removing the name does not by itself provide authorization
Removing a hospital number guarantees anonymity
Only a full patient name can identify someone
questions.explanation: Identifying details about patient, timing, or location can fit together, and de-identification is not authorization.

questions.stem: Which two questions should guide any decision to post or share a clinical image?
options: "Is it interesting?" and "Will it get likes?"
"Is the file small?" and "Is the caption short?"
"Did I remove the date?" and "Is it in black and white?"
"Could someone recognise this patient?" and "Am I authorised to use this information in this way?"
questions.explanation: Recognizability and authorization are the two required checks before any use of clinical information.

questions.stem: What should a student do if they realize they have already posted patient information without authorization?
options: Promptly tell their supervisor and follow the site's privacy breach process
Delete the post and say nothing
Wait to see whether anyone notices
Edit the caption and keep the post
questions.explanation: Prompt self-report allows containment; hiding the event prolongs the breach.

questions.stem: A student wants to use a real clinical case for a class presentation. What is the correct approach?
options: Take a photo during the scan and edit later
Confirm that the proposed use is authorized, follow the site's and school's approval process, and apply required de-identification and safeguards
Ask the patient verbally only, with no record
Use the case because it is for education
questions.explanation: Educational use requires authorization, the proper approval process, and de-identification safeguards.

questions.stem: Which statement about de-identification is correct?
options: Removing the name always guarantees anonymity
It requires more than deleting a name; approved processes and safeguards are needed
Captions never contribute to identification
Private groups make de-identification unnecessary
questions.explanation: Names are only one kind of identifying detail; approved de-identification must be applied.

questions.stem: Which statement about sharing a case in a private online group is correct?
options: Private groups are always authorized
Private groups are part of the circle of care
A private group still creates disclosure risks — screenshots and forwards cannot be controlled
Private groups eliminate the need for consent
questions.explanation: Information posted privately can still be captured and redistributed.

questions.stem: What is the core lesson of the reported case in which a nurse accessed thousands of patient records?
options: Curiosity does not become care because the user is a healthcare worker — an authorized purpose must support the access
Access is acceptable if no information is removed from the system
Only sharing constitutes a breach
Healthcare workers may access any record
questions.explanation: The central question is what authorized purpose supported the access — professional status does not supply one.

questions.stem: A record can be misused without being shared. What does this mean?
options: Only disclosure matters under privacy law
Viewing records is never a breach
Privacy rules apply only to emails
Unauthorized viewing or use alone can breach privacy obligations
questions.explanation: Privacy obligations attach to collection, use, and disclosure — not just sharing.

questions.stem: Which statement about clinical images used for teaching is correct?
options: Teaching use is automatically permitted
Only the student's own judgement is needed
Confirm authorization, follow the approval process, apply de-identification and security safeguards, and use approved teaching images when permission is uncertain
Photographs may be taken first and approved afterward
questions.explanation: Authorization and safeguards must be established before images are copied or shared.

questions.stem: Which statement about a patient's information in everyday conversation is TRUE?
options: Patient stories are acceptable if anonymous
A patient should never have to wonder whether something they shared during an echo will appear in someone's group chat
Conversations in break rooms are exempt
Names are the only protected detail
questions.explanation: The duty of confidentiality extends to casual conversation, documentation, and electronic systems.

questions.stem: Which practice best maintains confidentiality during an examination?
options: Limiting unnecessary exposure and interruptions and moving care conversations away from public areas
Leaving the door open for airflow
Discussing other patients during the scan
Allowing visitors to observe without permission
questions.explanation: Controlling exposure, interruptions, and the location of conversations protects confidentiality.

questions.stem: Which statement about confidentiality is correct?
options: It applies only to written records
It applies only to physicians
It applies only outside the workplace
It applies whether information is spoken, written, displayed on a screen, or stored as images
questions.explanation: The duty of confidentiality covers all forms in which patient information exists.

questions.stem: Why is privacy protection needed before information is ever sent anywhere?
options: Only sending information counts as a privacy event
Collection is never regulated
Privacy begins at discharge
Privacy obligations begin when information is collected, not only when a report is sent
questions.explanation: Collection and use are themselves governed steps, not just disclosure.

questions.stem: You realize you sent patient information by fax to the wrong number. What is the FIRST response?
options: Stop further unauthorized access or disclosure and follow the organization's immediate containment steps
Keep sending it until it goes through
Say nothing and hope the recipient ignores it
Alter the record to show nothing was sent
questions.explanation: Further disclosure must stop and the organization's containment steps must be followed immediately.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: After containment, what should be reported?
options: Report only if the patient complains
Report promptly through the privacy and supervisory process, describing the facts accurately
Report to social media for transparency
Wait a week to see the outcome
questions.explanation: Prompt reporting through designated privacy channels, with accurate facts, is required.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: Which information belongs in a breach report?
options: Speculation about who is to blame
What happened, which information was involved, when it occurred, and what has been done so far
A guess about whether harm will occur
Nothing — verbal reports are sufficient
questions.explanation: The report should contain the facts: event, information involved, timing, and actions taken.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: Which action must be avoided after a suspected breach?
options: Quietly hiding the event or altering records to make it look as though it never occurred
Following containment steps
Reporting promptly
Cooperating with the privacy contact
questions.explanation: Concealment or alteration of records compounds the breach and can constitute misconduct.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: Who assesses a privacy breach and handles required notifications?
options: The individual staff member alone
The custodian or organization, through its designated privacy process
The patient's family
Social media platforms
questions.explanation: The individual's role is to report and cooperate; the custodian assesses and notifies as required.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: What is the practitioner's role after reporting a breach?
options: Cooperate and follow instructions for containment and documentation rather than independently deciding the information was harmless
Decide personally that the information was harmless and stop the process
Destroy related records
Wait for a lawsuit
questions.explanation: The practitioner reports and cooperates; the assessment of risk and notifications follow the organization's process.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: Why should you not continue troubleshooting a disclosure error alone?
options: Continuing to send or forward information while working it out alone can extend the unauthorized disclosure
Mistakes require no response
Isolation improves accuracy
Only the patient may report it
questions.explanation: Unauthorized transmission should stop immediately rather than continue during troubleshooting.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: A colleague suggests simply deleting the evidence of an accidental disclosure. Why is this wrong?
options: Deletion is inefficient
Concealing or altering records to hide an event is prohibited and can amount to professional misconduct
Storage space is limited
Records must be kept for marketing purposes
questions.explanation: Records must never be altered or concealed to make an event appear not to have occurred.
tags: Responding to a Suspected Privacy Breach

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the primary everyday purpose of the clinical record?
options: Building a case against the practitioner
Marketing the department
Satisfying curiosity
Supporting safe, continuous patient care and communication among the care team
questions.explanation: The record's everyday purpose is safe, continuous care — though it may later be reviewed in a complaint or legal proceeding.

questions.stem: Which qualities must clinical record entries possess?
options: Accurate, complete, timely and attributable
Verbose, subjective, delayed and anonymous
Informal, partial, backdated and unsigned
Opinionated, negative, vague and optional
questions.explanation: Entries must be accurate, complete, timely, and attributable to be a reliable record.

questions.stem: Which set of items belongs in the clinical record?
options: Personal opinions about the patient's attitude
The examination and what was completed, relevant observations and attributed patient reports, limitations and their reasons, actions, patient response and follow-up communication
Only normal findings
Only the sonographer's initials
questions.explanation: These are the categories of information that describe the care that actually occurred.

questions.stem: A sonographer could not obtain several required images. What should the record say?
options: Nothing, because the gap is obvious
That the examination was complete
Which views could not be obtained, the reason, and who was notified
That the patient refused everything
questions.explanation: Specific limitations, reasons, and communication must be documented; an omitted part must never be suggested as normal.

questions.stem: Which entry correctly separates a patient report from an observation?
options: "The patient is dizzy and uncooperative."
"Dizzy for no reason."
"Probably dehydrated."
"Patient reports dizziness when sitting up."
questions.explanation: Attribution to the patient's report distinguishes it from the practitioner's own observations.

questions.stem: Why is the entry "Patient was anxious and difficult to scan" inadequate?
options: It is too long
It labels the person instead of describing what the patient reported and what was done
It contains medical terms
It identifies the patient
questions.explanation: Labels communicate the writer's frustration rather than facts the next clinician can use.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD cannot hold their breath for imaging. Which documentation is most appropriate?
options: "Patient refused to cooperate."
"Patient did not understand."
"Poor study due to patient attitude."
"Patient unable to comply with respiration."
questions.explanation: Describing what was observed — without inventing a reason — is specific and factual.

questions.stem: What should you do if you do not know why a patient could not complete a maneuver?
options: Assume a reason and document it as fact
Write "patient refused" as a default
Leave the record blank
Describe what you observed and what the patient said; do not invent a reason
questions.explanation: You can be concise and still be specific — never invent an explanation.

questions.stem: Robin reports shoulder pain in a position, scanning pauses, Robin agrees to continue differently, and some images cannot be obtained. Which entry best reflects what happened?
options: "Patient difficult. Study incomplete."
"Study completed as planned."

"Patient reported shoulder pain in the initial position. Scanning was paused and patient assisted to sit upright. Patient agreed to continue in a different position. Some planned images could not be obtained."
"Position changed for no clear reason."
questions.explanation: The entry records the report, the action, the patient's agreement, and the actual limitation.

questions.stem: Why should specific limited views be named in a real record?
options: To make the record longer
Because naming views is legally prohibited
So the record can be deleted later
So the interpreting physician knows exactly what can and cannot be concluded
questions.explanation: Specificity lets the interpreting physician judge what conclusions the study supports.

questions.stem: A sonographer is tempted to add "cardiologist notified" to a note because it would look good. What is the correct standard?
options: Add it if it will likely happen
Add it if a colleague agrees
Add it to impress the reader
Only document what is true — the entry must match what actually happened
questions.explanation: Documentation must reflect reality — never claim an action that did not occur.

questions.stem: How should an error discovered after an entry was saved be corrected?
options: Silently replace the entry so the original disappears
Use the approved correction or addendum process so the change remains attributable and traceable
Overwrite without an audit trail
Delete the entire record
questions.explanation: Corrections must preserve the original and be traceable to the person and time of the change.

questions.stem: A late entry is made two days after an event. What must it distinguish?
options: The writer's opinion from the patient's
The time of the event from the time of the entry
The day of the week from the shift
Nothing — late entries are prohibited entirely
questions.explanation: An approved late entry must clearly distinguish when the event occurred from when it was documented.

questions.stem: What is the professional consequence risk of falsifying information in a record?
options: Falsifying information may amount to professional misconduct
No consequence exists without a lawsuit
It is acceptable if it protects the department
It is acceptable if no harm resulted
questions.explanation: Falsification is a professional conduct issue independent of whether any lawsuit follows.

questions.stem: Who should a record entry be attributable to?
options: The department as a whole
The interpreting physician only
The person who made the entry, identified per the system, usually by initials
Nobody — anonymous entries are preferred
questions.explanation: Attribution identifies who wrote the entry, which is essential for traceability.

questions.stem: Before finalizing a study, which checks should be completed?
options: Only the patient's room number
Only the machine settings
Identifiers, values, and whether the completion status matches the study
No checks are needed
questions.explanation: Final checks confirm the right patient, correct values, and accurate completion status.

questions.stem: Why should an entry be written right after the echo?
options: To keep the sonographer busy
Timely documentation preserves accurate detail and makes the record available for immediate clinical decisions
Because records may only be written during the scan
To delay communication
questions.explanation: Details fade quickly; timely documentation preserves accuracy and supports immediate decisions.

questions.stem: Who is the intended audience of a clinical record?
options: Only the sonographer
Anyone who may legitimately read it later — another clinician, the patient, an investigator, or even a court
Only the department manager
Only the interpreter
questions.explanation: Entries should be written so a reader months later can understand what happened without being able to ask questions.

questions.stem: Which statement about a clinical record and legal proceedings is correct?
options: The record exists only for lawsuits
A good note guarantees a particular legal outcome
The record may become evidence of what was observed, explained, and done, while its everyday purpose remains safe, continuous care
Records have no evidentiary value
questions.explanation: The record can serve as evidence, but it is primarily the tool of everyday care.

questions.stem: Which statement about documentation and incident reporting is correct?
options: Correcting the record replaces any safety report
Safety reports replace clinical documentation
Correcting the clinical record does not automatically complete a separate safety reporting obligation
Neither is required if no harm occurred
questions.explanation: Each process has a distinct purpose, and completing one does not discharge the other.

questions.stem: Which legislation provides the framework for consent to treatment in an echo appointment?
options: PHIPA
The Health Care Consent Act
The Child, Youth and Family Services Act
The Municipal Freedom of Information Act
questions.explanation: Consent to treatment — including imaging procedures — is governed by the HCCA.

questions.stem: Which TWO things must happen before an echo begins?
options: Obtain payment and schedule the next appointment
Explain the examination, and check that the patient understands and agrees to proceed
Complete the report and file the images
Verify insurance and collect a deposit
questions.explanation: Explanation plus verification of understanding and agreement are the two required pre-examination steps.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for valid consent?
options: It is confirmed by a family member's signature in every case
It relates to the proposed procedure
It is informed
It is voluntary
questions.explanation: The four requirements are that consent relates to the procedure, is informed, is voluntary, and is not obtained through misrepresentation or fraud.

questions.stem: What does it mean that consent must "relate to the proposed procedure"?
options: Any consent covers every future procedure
Saying yes to an echo does not automatically mean saying yes to another procedure, such as adding contrast
Only verbal consent relates to the procedure
Consent may never be extended
questions.explanation: Agreement is procedure-specific; additional procedures require their own agreement.

questions.stem: Which requirement is most clearly missing when a patient agrees after hearing, "It'll just take a minute. Don't worry about it," with no explanation of the echo?
options: Informed consent
Voluntary consent
Written consent
Substitute consent
questions.explanation: Without information about what the examination involves, the consent is not informed.

questions.stem: Which information is needed for a decision to be informed?
options: Only the name of the procedure
Only the cost
Only the appointment time
What the procedure involves and its expected benefit, material risks and side effects, reasonable alternatives, and the likely consequences of declining
questions.explanation: These categories allow the patient to weigh benefits, risks, alternatives, and consequences.

questions.stem: Which question must a patient be able to answer to give informed consent?
options: What is the sonographer's schedule?
Which machine brand will be used?
What is the department's wait time?
What will happen and how could it help me?
questions.explanation: The four required questions concern what will happen and its benefit, discomforts or risks, alternatives, and the consequences of waiting or declining.

questions.stem: What could happen if I say nothing, wait, or say no?" is one of the four informed-consent questions. What must the answer avoid?
options: Honesty
Detail
Pressure — the consequences of declining should be explained without feeling pressured
Reference to alternatives
questions.explanation: Consequences must be presented factually without coercing the patient's decision.

questions.stem: Which statement about consent forms is correct?
options: A signature automatically establishes informed consent
Forms replace explanation entirely
A signature alone does not prove that the requirements for valid consent have been met
Forms eliminate the need to check understanding
questions.explanation: A form records a decision but cannot replace the information and voluntary choice required for validity.

questions.stem: What is wrong with telling a patient, "You have to do this because the doctor ordered it"?
options: It is technically inaccurate
It undermines voluntariness — agreement obtained through pressure does not demonstrate respect for the patient's choice
Nothing — it is an acceptable explanation
It replaces the need for information
questions.explanation: Pressure from authority compromises the voluntary nature of consent.

questions.stem: When must consent be maintained?
options: Only at the start
Only at the end
Throughout the entire procedure — it is an ongoing process
Only if the patient asks questions
questions.explanation: Consent continues through the examination; the patient must remain willing to continue.

questions.stem: Why is checking understanding important after providing information?
options: It is a test of the patient's intelligence
It is optional in routine examinations
Giving someone information is only useful if they can make sense of it
It replaces written documentation
questions.explanation: Checking understanding — without making the patient feel tested — confirms the consent is informed.

questions.stem: Which technique best checks understanding in plain language?
options: "I just want to make sure I explained that clearly. Do you have any questions?"
"Do you understand?"
"Sign here, please."
"Any questions? No? Good."
questions.explanation: The phrasing checks the clarity of the explanation rather than putting the patient on the spot.

questions.stem: Which explanation uses appropriate plain language?
options: "Assume the left lateral decubitus position"
"We will now optimize the acoustic window"
"I'll help you lie on your left side"
"Prepare for apical four-chamber acquisition"
questions.explanation: Everyday words one step at a time support understanding far better than technical jargon.

questions.stem: What must happen regarding the student's role in the examination?
options: The student may scan without introduction
The role only needs to be documented afterward
The patient must be told the student's role and give agreement for their involvement
The patient never needs to know
questions.explanation: The patient should always understand who is doing what.

questions.stem: Which statement about consent to the examination versus consent to share information is correct?
options: They are the same consent
Only PHIPA applies to the procedure
Only the HCCA applies to information sharing
The HCCA concerns the procedure; PHIPA concerns access to and sharing of information
questions.explanation: Saying yes to an echo does not mean saying yes to sharing results with everyone.

questions.stem: When facing a question about consent, what is the first step?
options: Assume it concerns the examination
Identify what the consent concerns — the examination or the information
Assume it concerns the information
Refuse to answer
questions.explanation: Distinguishing treatment consent from information consent directs you to the right framework.

questions.stem: Who has primary responsibility for informed consent and capacity for a proposed treatment?
options: The sonographer performing the ordered examination alone
The practitioner proposing the treatment
The patient's family
The scheduling clerk
questions.explanation: The proposing practitioner holds primary responsibility, while the sonographer still explains and maintains agreement.

questions.stem: What are the two components of capacity for a decision?
options: Understand the relevant information, and appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of the choice
Be an adult, and have a signed form
Be alert, and agree with the physician
Have insurance, and be registered
questions.explanation: Capacity requires both understanding the relevant information and appreciating how the consequences apply to one's own situation.

questions.stem: Why is appreciating consequences important for capacity?
options: It only concerns remembering appointment times
It guarantees agreement with the recommendation
It is unrelated to the decision
It includes recognizing what could happen if the person says no
questions.explanation: A person must recognize how possible consequences — including declining — apply to their own situation.

questions.stem: Which statement about capacity is correct?
options: Capacity is permanent once granted
Capacity depends only on chronological age
Capacity depends only on diagnosis
Capacity is specific to the decision and to the time
questions.explanation: A person may be able to decide about one procedure but not another, and ability can change over time.

questions.stem: What is the starting presumption about a patient's capacity?
options: Assume capacity unless there are reasonable grounds for concern
Assume incapacity until proven otherwise
Assume incapacity for anyone over 65
Assume incapacity whenever a diagnosis exists
questions.explanation: The presumption of capacity is the starting point; age or diagnosis alone does not settle the question.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old understands the proposed echo and its consequences. What is the correct understanding?
options: A parent must always consent for a minor
Only a judge may decide
Age 17 has no relevance in Ontario
Being under 18 does not automatically mean a parent must decide
questions.explanation: If the young person understands and appreciates the decision, they may be able to consent.

questions.stem: A patient has a diagnosis of dementia. What is the correct approach?
options: The diagnosis alone does not decide whether the person can make this particular decision today — assess the decision-specific understanding and appreciation
Treat the diagnosis as proof of incapacity
Automatically ask a relative to decide
Use chronological age as the deciding factor
questions.explanation: Capacity must be assessed for the specific decision at the specific time.

questions.stem: A patient cannot understand the explanation given in English. What should happen BEFORE any conclusion about capacity?
options: Conclude they lack capacity
Ask a family member to decide without support
Cancel the examination permanently
Arrange an appropriate interpreter or communication support
questions.explanation: Language difficulty does not by itself show inability to decide; communication barriers must be addressed first.

questions.stem: A patient understands all the relevant information but still declines the recommended examination. What does this mean?
options: The patient must lack capacity
Refusing a recommendation does not automatically mean the patient lacks capacity
The refusal must be ignored
A substitute decision-maker must be used immediately
questions.explanation: A capable person is entitled to make a choice that differs from the recommendation.

questions.stem: Who determines capacity for a proposed treatment?
options: The sonographer performing the examination alone
The practitioner proposing the treatment
The patient's family
The registration clerk
questions.explanation: The practitioner proposing the treatment determines capacity for that treatment.

questions.stem: If a student is concerned about a patient's understanding, what should they do?
options: Pause and tell the supervisor exactly what they have noticed
Decide independently that the patient lacks capacity
Proceed without mentioning it
Ask the patient to leave
questions.explanation: Students pause and report their specific observations to the supervisor rather than deciding alone.

questions.stem: What is a substitute decision-maker (SDM)?
options: Any relative who volunteers
The sonographer's supervisor
The patient's friend
A person legally authorized to make decisions for a patient who cannot make the particular decision
questions.explanation: The SDM must be legally authorized for that decision, and the authority's limits must be confirmed.

questions.stem: A patient can decide about one aspect of care but not another. What does this illustrate?
options: Capacity is irrelevant
Capacity is decision-specific
Capacity is permanent
Capacity depends on insurance
questions.explanation: The ability to decide varies with the particular decision being made.

questions.stem: Which statement about capacity and time is TRUE?
options: A capacity assessment from years ago always applies
Capacity never changes once established
Time of assessment is irrelevant
A person's ability can change over time, so capacity must be assessed when the decision is made
questions.explanation: Because capacity can fluctuate, it must be evaluated at the time of the specific decision.

questions.stem: What should a sonographer do while remaining within their role when capacity is in question?
options: Make the capacity determination independently
Ignore concerns to avoid delay
Check and maintain consent, and bring unresolved concerns to the supervising or responsible practitioner
Ask the family to overrule the patient
questions.explanation: The sonographer maintains consent vigilance while the proposing practitioner determines capacity.

questions.stem: What is express consent?
options: The person directly communicates that they agree, verbally or in writing
Arrival at the clinic
Silence during the explanation
Lying on the examination bed
questions.explanation: Express consent is a direct statement of agreement, which may be verbal or written.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates express consent?
options: A patient arrives at the hospital
A patient does not object while staff talk nearby
After an explanation, a patient says, "Yes, you may begin."
A patient remains silent in the waiting room
questions.explanation: Express consent is a direct, clearly communicated agreement — verbal or written — after the patient has been informed.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: Which statement about verbal and written express consent is correct?
options: Only written consent is ever valid
Only verbal consent is ever valid
Neither requires information or voluntariness
Both are valid provided the patient understands and chooses freely
questions.explanation: Both forms are valid when the underlying requirements of valid consent are met.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: What determines whether written consent must be obtained?
options: The patient's preference alone
The procedure and workplace policy, including documentation requirements
The sonographer's comfort
The time of day
questions.explanation: Procedure-specific requirements and workplace policy determine the form and documentation of consent.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: What is implied consent?
options: Silence in every situation
Arrival for any appointment
Absence of verbal objection
A person's actions show agreement when the situation makes their meaning clear
questions.explanation: Implied consent depends on conduct that clearly indicates agreement in context.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: After an explanation, a patient willingly turns onto their left side to begin the echo. What does this illustrate?
options: Express written consent
Implied consent — conduct that clearly indicates agreement in context
Fraud
Emergency consent
questions.explanation: Willingly positioning for the examination is conduct that clearly signals agreement after explanation.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: Which statement about implied consent is correct?
options: Implied consent removes the need for explanation
Implied consent applies to any disclosure
All requirements for valid consent still apply to implied consent
Implied consent never requires context
questions.explanation: Implied consent must still be informed, voluntary, and related to the procedure.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about silence?
options: Silence alone does not give permission to scan
Silence equals full consent
Silence waives the right to stop later
Silence establishes consent to share information
questions.explanation: Silence, arrival, or lying on the bed without resistance does not establish agreement.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: What habit best secures agreement before scanning begins?
options: Begin silently and document later
Assume agreement from the order
Assume agreement from the appointment
Explain, answer questions, and ask, "May I begin?"
questions.explanation: An explicit, plain-language request for permission makes agreement clear and documented.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: The patient hesitates and pulls away slightly. What should the sonographer do?
options: Pause and check — "Are you comfortable with me continuing?"
Continue because they agreed earlier
Continue because the order exists
Finish the current view first
questions.explanation: When agreement seems unclear, the practitioner must ask rather than assume.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: Which framework applies to consent to share patient information with a third party?
options: The HCCA alone
PHIPA and the authorized processes for disclosure
The scheduling policy
The equipment manual
questions.explanation: Consent to share information is governed by PHIPA, distinct from consent to treatment.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts consent to care and consent to share?
options: The two questions are identical
Only the second question matters
"Do you agree to the proposed echocardiogram?" concerns the procedure; "What authority allows this information to be accessed or shared?" concerns the information
Only the first question matters
questions.explanation: The first is a treatment-consent question under the HCCA; the second is an information question under PHIPA.
tags: Express Consent, Implied Consent, and Consent to Share

questions.stem: During an echo, a patient says they are uncomfortable and asks you to stop. What is the best immediate response?
options: Continue because they agreed at the beginning
Stop scanning and attend to their comfort and safety
Finish the current view before stopping
Document their concern and continue
questions.explanation: Consent is ongoing — an immediate request to stop must be honoured right away.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Which statement captures the rule about stopping?
options: Required images override the patient's request
Required images do not give permission to continue after the patient asks us to stop
The order overrides the patient's request
Stopping requires a physician's order
questions.explanation: Completing required images never justifies continuing after a request to stop.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: What is the best first statement to a patient who says, "Please stop"?
options: "Of course we can stop. Tell me what's uncomfortable. Let me get my team lead."
"We only need a few more images."
"You signed up for this."
"The doctor wants it finished."
questions.explanation: The response stops scanning, acknowledges the request, and involves the supervisor without pressure.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: After stopping, which question best clarifies the patient's wishes without pressure?
options: "Why are you making this difficult?"
"Do you want to finish quickly?"
"Would you like a break, a different position, or just to stop the echo altogether?"
"Should I tell the doctor you refused?"
questions.explanation: Offering clear options lets the patient choose without having to justify their decision first.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Does the patient need to explain WHY they want to stop before you stop?
options: No — you stop first, then clarify their wishes
Yes — an explanation is required before stopping
Yes — only a physician may approve stopping
Yes — documentation must precede stopping
questions.explanation: The request itself governs; explanation comes afterward.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Which action must be avoided after a patient asks to stop?
options: Checking the patient's comfort
Involving the supervisor
Documenting what happened
Continuing to scan while asking questions, or trying to obtain "one more image"
questions.explanation: Scanning must stop immediately — no images should be obtained while the request is being addressed.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: The patient now appears calm and agrees to a break. What is required before scanning resumes?
options: The patient understands the plan and freely re-establishes consent
A calmer appearance alone
The supervisor's approval alone
The completion of the schedule
questions.explanation: Looking more comfortable does not automatically mean the patient wants to continue.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: What must be documented when scanning is stopped by the patient?
options: Only that the study was incomplete
Why scanning stopped, what was done, whether the patient agreed to restart, whether the study was completed, limitations, and communication
Only the patient's name
Nothing until the next visit
questions.explanation: A complete record covers the stop, the response, any restart, completion status, limitations, and communication.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: A capable patient decides not to complete the remaining images. What should the sonographer do?
options: Respect the decision, document and communicate for appropriate follow-up
Resume once the patient appears calmer
Ask a relative to overrule the patient
Finish because an order remains in place
questions.explanation: The capable patient's decision must be respected, with documentation, communication, and appropriate follow-up.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Which response to a patient declining an examination is best?
options: "You have no choice — it's ordered."
"Fine, but your doctor will be angry."
"Would you like to tell me what concerns you about the echo?" — listen, answer within your role, and involve the appropriate clinician if needed
Argue until the patient agrees
questions.explanation: Exploring the concern calmly, answering within role, and involving the clinician respects the patient without pressure.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: A patient continues to decline after discussion. What is required?
options: Continue persuading until they agree
Perform the examination because an order exists
Respect the decision, avoid argument or pressure, inform the supervisor, and document the decision and discussion
Tell the patient to leave
questions.explanation: The refusal is respected and documented, with the supervisor informed.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Which documentation wording is appropriately factual about a refusal?
options: "Patient declined the examination," with the relevant discussion and communication recorded
"Patient was uncooperative."
"Patient refused for no reason."
"Study not done."
questions.explanation: Factual wording records the decision and discussion without judgment.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: An echo is ordered as a stat examination. What does the urgency establish?
options: Nothing about permission by itself — calling an echo urgent or stat does not automatically authorize performing it
Automatic consent to everything
That consent may be skipped entirely
That the sonographer may override a refusal
questions.explanation: Urgency does not replace consent; the emergency conditions must actually apply.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Which statement about emergency exceptions is correct?
options: Any urgent order creates an emergency exception
Being behind schedule creates an emergency exception
A busy department creates an emergency exception
The HCCA provides specific emergency exceptions, and urgency alone does not establish that an exception applies
questions.explanation: The exceptions have specific conditions; schedule pressure or a stat order does not satisfy them.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Who checks whether the emergency consent rules apply?
options: The sonographer alone
The patient's family
The responsible clinician, including checking any known earlier refusal
The scheduling clerk
questions.explanation: The responsible clinician verifies whether the emergency rules apply, including any prior refusal.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: A capable patient is able to make and communicate their decision during an emergency. What must be respected?
options: The order alone
The schedule
The family's preference over the patient's
Their refusal — a capable patient's refusal still matters
questions.explanation: If a capable patient can decide and communicate, their refusal must be respected even in an urgent setting.
tags: Refusal, Withdrawal, Pausing and Emergency Exceptions

questions.stem: Jordan arrives with a partner and asks, "Please talk to me privately about my health." What should happen first?
options: Include the partner automatically because they drove Jordan
Speak with Jordan privately and, if the partner is to be involved, ask Jordan directly whether that is acceptable
Refuse to speak with either of them
Tell the partner everything for efficiency
questions.explanation: Jordan's privacy request is respected, and permission for the partner's involvement is sought from Jordan.

questions.stem: Later, the partner asks, "What did the scan show?" What could you say without sharing results?
options: The full findings, because the partner is family
"Everything is normal."
"I understand your concern. I need to check what Jordan would like shared, and the clinical team will explain results through the usual process."
Nothing at all, rudely
questions.explanation: The response acknowledges concern, checks authority, and points to the proper results process.

questions.stem: Which statement about family and information is correct?
options: Being someone's partner or family member does not automatically establish permission to receive information
Family members always have full access
Family access depends only on their persistence
Family access depends on their relationship length
questions.explanation: A family relationship alone does not constitute lawful authority to receive information.

questions.stem: During scanning, Jordan says, "Please stop. This is uncomfortable." What is the correct response?
options: Explain why the remaining images are needed before stopping
Stop scanning promptly and safely, acknowledge the request, and involve the supervising sonographer
Reduce pressure and continue
Pause briefly and resume once Jordan appears calmer
questions.explanation: The student stops, acknowledges, and involves the supervisor; the request governs what happens next.

questions.stem: After a discussion with the supervisor, Jordan decides to end the examination. What is required?
options: Continue scanning because the order remains
Ask the partner to overrule Jordan
Record the study as complete
Respect the decision and arrange appropriate follow-up
questions.explanation: Jordan's decision ends the examination, and follow-up must be arranged.

questions.stem: In the hallway, the partner asks for the results. What is the most defensible response?
options: Acknowledge the partner's concern and check Jordan's permission or other lawful authority before sharing anything
Share the results because they are in the hallway
Share only the normal parts
Shout the results so others can hear
questions.explanation: Concern is acknowledged while authority to disclose is verified first.

questions.stem: What should Jordan's record contain after the examination ends early?
options: Jordan's request to stop, the response, the incomplete study, and the actual communication
Only "Study completed."
Only Jordan's name
The partner's account of events
questions.explanation: The record must accurately describe the request, response, what remained incomplete, and communication.

questions.stem: A record states only "Study completed" when the patient's request to stop was not honoured. What would a reviewer need?
options: Nothing more
The patient's request, the response, what was completed and not completed, who was informed, and follow-up
The sonographer's opinion of the patient
The partner's signature
questions.explanation: A reviewer needs the facts of the request, response, completion status, and communication.

questions.stem: The partner pressures Jordan before the examination: "Just agree. We're holding everyone up." Which consent requirement is at risk?
options: Voluntariness — agreement obtained through pressure does not demonstrate respect for choice
Informed consent only
Written consent only
Implied consent only
questions.explanation: Coercion by a companion compromises the voluntary nature of consent.

questions.stem: Once the partner steps out, what is an appropriate next statement?
options: "We can pause and talk. What concerns you about having the echo today?"
"Your partner is right — we are busy."
"You must decide now."
"I cannot discuss this with you."
questions.explanation: The statement opens a private, pressure-free conversation about the patient's concerns.

questions.stem: Jordan asks whether the echo can wait. What is the most appropriate response?
options: "Delaying is completely safe."
"Waiting will definitely make things worse."
"I'll ask the clinician responsible for your care to explain what waiting can mean for you" — without promising that delay is safe
"You have no option but today."
questions.explanation: The sonographer connects the patient to the clinician who can explain consequences, without making unsupported promises.

questions.stem: A colleague says the examination must proceed because "every department is busy." What is the correct understanding?
options: Busyness creates an emergency exception
Busyness allows skipping consent
Schedule pressure never substitutes for consent or justifies coercion
Busyness permits overriding a refusal
questions.explanation: Being behind schedule does not create an emergency exception or excuse pressure.

questions.stem: Which framework applies when the partner asks who may receive the report?
options: The HCCA alone
Equipment policy
The scheduling system
PHIPA and authorized processes
questions.explanation: Disclosure decisions are governed by PHIPA and authorized processes.

questions.stem: Which framework applies when Jordan asks to stop the examination?
options: PHIPA alone
The billing code
The HCCA and consent standards
Workplace seniority
questions.explanation: The right to stop is a consent-to-treatment matter under the HCCA.

questions.stem: Which framework applies when documenting what actually happened?
options: CMRITO documentation standards
PHIPA alone
The CYFSA
The RHPA reporting provisions
questions.explanation: Documentation expectations come from the regulator's standards.

questions.stem: Which statement about applying these frameworks is correct?
options: Only one law can ever apply
More than one set of rules can apply at the same time
Laws never overlap
Standards replace all legislation
questions.explanation: A single situation — such as Jordan's — can engage PHIPA, the HCCA, and documentation standards simultaneously.

questions.stem: Which set best matches the four closing duties taught for this case?
options: Protect privacy, respect choices, record the facts, speak up
Move fast, avoid questions, document little, stay silent
Share widely, pressure gently, record rarely, remain quiet
Diagnose, prescribe, discharge, forget
questions.explanation: The four duties — protect information, listen to the patient, write honestly, and ask for help — summarize the case.

questions.stem: An unrelated coworker asks to see Jordan's images "just to learn." What is the best response?
options: Share because they work in the same department
Share if they whisper
"I can't share Jordan's images for that purpose. If you're interested in learning, we can look at an approved teaching example."
Share the images but not the report
questions.explanation: Working in the same organization does not authorize access; approved teaching materials serve learning properly.

questions.stem: Which combination represents a fully defensible response to Jordan's case?
options: Finish the study, tell the partner everything, and document only the findings
Stop the study, tell the partner nothing rudely, and document nothing
Let the partner decide what to record

Respect the decision to end the examination and arrange follow-up; acknowledge the partner's concern and check authority before sharing; record the request, response, incomplete study, and actual communication
questions.explanation: The defensible response covers the examination, the partner, and the record.

questions.stem: What is the underlying principle connecting privacy, consent, and documentation in Jordan's case?
options: The patient trusts the practitioner to protect their information, respect their choices, record what happened, and speak up when needed
Efficiency should govern all three
